target_customer: US consumers, especially younger and lower balance savers, who respond to lottery style prizes more than to interest rates
problem: Many Americans do not save; prize linked savings (like UK Premium Bonds) gamble on small prizes to motivate deposits without risking principal.
business_model: Interest spread on deposits held at partner banks, with prizes funded from the spread; later gaming style products and sweepstakes games

founders.name: Adam Moelis
founders.background_notes: Per YC page. Wikiwand and other coverage describe him as the son of Ken Moelis, founder of Moelis and Company.

founders.name: Ben Doyle
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder on the YC page and in the Blazer interview coverage; no background listed.

competitors.name: Long Game
competitors.what: Prize linked savings app where deposits earn virtual coins to play lottery style games, accounts run with Blue Ridge Bank
competitors.traction_then: Nearly 70,000 users who add about 60 dollars a month, per founder in May 2017

technical_complexity.rationale: Banking as a service integration plus a random drawing mechanic; hard parts were compliance with prize linked savings rules and the bank partner, not core engineering.

defensibility.rationale: The idea was borrowed from UK Premium Bonds and Long Game existed since 2015; relied on a partner bank and word of mouth with no deep lock in.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent copied the weekly 10 million dollar drawing. The bigger shock came from the banking partner chain: the Synapse collapse in 2024 froze deposits.

market_need_then: Low US savings habits and near zero bank interest in 2020 made a prize hook plausible; Yotta reported 40,000 new customers and over 40 million dollars of deposits in under four months by October 2020.

branding.name_origin: Not explained in sources. The company first went by Benjamin and dropped it because a financial product is heavily googled and ranking for a common word would be hard, per the Blazer interview.

identity.voice_and_tone: Upbeat, short all caps slogans such as Play games, win big

branding.brand_signature: The weekly chance to win up to 10 million dollars

rebrands.why: A common word would be hard to rank for in search, per the CEO in a Blazer interview

branding.community_and_virality: Reported growth largely through word of mouth in 2020 (PYMNTS); a Reddit IAmA by the CEO in December 2020 appears in search.

brand_strength.rationale: Memorable hook and strong early word of mouth; later brand shifted to casino style games and was tied to the Synapse frozen funds news.

pivots.to: Free to play games and sweepstakes style prizes
pivots.why: Not stated by the company in sources; the current site markets games with prizes and secondary sources tie the shift to the 2024 Synapse and Evolve crisis

outcome_analysis: Yotta grew fast in 2020 on word of mouth with a prize linked savings hook, raised a 3.3M seed and a 13.2M Series A in January 2021, and is still listed Active. Its fate turned on its banking stack: the 2024 Synapse bankruptcy and Evolve Bank problems left about 85,000 customers with roughly 112 million dollars unreachable, led to class actions and a Yotta lawsuit against Evolve, and the product moved toward games. The company survives but not as the original savings brand.
notes: Seed and Series A were each found in two or more outlets (fintech.global and Crunchbase News for the seed; Wikipedia for the Series A), but the Series A date comes from search summaries and the Series A article itself was not opened. Crunchbase total of 16.6M across three rounds suggests a third small round or YC amount not itemized. Founder Ben Doyle is sometimes mixed up in queries with other names; only Doyle and Moelis are sourced. Pivot date is approximate. Yotta is not an exit or a shutdown, and failure factors reflect the Synapse related losses, not a collapse of the company.
